title: Transfer Dynamics and Spectral Cascades in Graph-Coupled Kuramoto Networks
authors: Marcin Kowalczyk, Pietro Liò, Zbigniew R. Struzik
abstract: This work introduces a spectral transfer formalism for nonlinear synchronisation dynamics to resolve how internal dynamical activity redistributes across network scales, moving beyond traditional global observables like the Kuramoto order parameter. By projecting Kuramoto phase dynamics onto the eigenbasis of the graph Laplacian, we construct a time-dependent transfer matrix and derive novel network metrics, including the spectral flux, which quantifies directional redistribution between structural dynamical scales rather than physical transport across nodes. Numerical simulations on modular and hierarchical networks reveal highly structured, intermittent spectral transfer episodes characterised by forward and inverse spectral cascades, directional reversals, and complex interaction geometries. Crucially, we demonstrate a clear separation between macroscopic coherence and microscopic spectral interactions, showing that highly organised, fluctuating internal redistribution dynamics persist even beneath nearly stationary and featureless global synchronisation states. This framework extends conventional synchronisation analysis and establishes a multiscale approach for interpreting network dynamics as an evolving process of spectral reorganisation.
summary: This paper develops a spectral transfer formalism to analyze nonlinear synchronization in coupled oscillator networks, moving beyond simple global measures. By projecting dynamics onto the graph Laplacian eigenbasis, the authors quantify how activity redistributes across structural scales via a transfer matrix. This reveals hidden, structured spectral reorganizations that persist even when the overall system appears macroscopically stable.
main_problem: The work aims to resolve how internal dynamical activity redistributes across network scales during nonlinear synchronization, moving beyond traditional global observables like the Kuramoto order parameter.
main_result: The study demonstrates a clear separation between macroscopic coherence and microscopic spectral interactions, showing that structured, fluctuating internal redistribution dynamics persist even when global synchronisation is nearly stationary.
method: A spectral transfer formalism is introduced by projecting Kuramoto phase dynamics onto the eigenbasis of the graph Laplacian, constructing a time-dependent transfer matrix.
model_or_system: The model uses the Kuramoto oscillator system coupled on a general graph structure, with analysis focusing on modular and hierarchical network architectures.
key_observables: Spectral flux, Spectral Modal Energy ($E_m(t)$), Transfer Matrix elements ($T_{m 	o k}(t)$), Net Spectral Flux ($\Pi(t, K_0)$), and the conventional Kuramoto order parameter ($R(t)$).
important_parameters: Coupling strength ($K$), frequency heterogeneity ($\sigma_{\omega}$), and the structural scales defined by the graph Laplacian eigenmodes.
main_assumptions: The spectral flux quantifies redistribution between *structural* dynamical scales defined by the Laplacian eigenbasis, not physical transport across nodes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate graph spectral decomposition (showing mode hierarchies) and the temporal evolution of spectral activity, including cross-sections of the transfer matrix and the spectral flux ($\Pi$).
paper_structure: The paper builds the spectral transfer formalism by decomposing the state onto graph eigenmodes, constructing the transfer matrix to quantify mode exchange, and analyzing the resulting spectral flux and various transfer observables to characterize different dynamical regimes.
why_interesting: The concept of spectral reorganisation and the separation of global coherence from underlying spectral dynamics provides a powerful, multiscale diagnostic tool applicable to analyzing complex, non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body systems, which is relevant to open quantum systems.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Illustration of graph spectral decomposition. (a) Example of a random network. (b) Laplacian spectrum of the network shown in panel (a), with graph frequencies ordered by eigenvalue. (c) First non-trivial Laplacian eigenvector of the same network, representing a low-frequency graph mode associated with large-scale structural organisation. (d) Highest-frequency Laplacian eigenvector of the network, representing fine-scale variation across the graph. Together, panels (b)–(d) illustrate how the network structure shown in panel (a) gives rise to a hierarchy of graph-spectral modes that form the basis of the graph Fourier representation used throughout this work.

Fig. 2 Illustration of the modular network architecture used throughout this study. (a) Example of a modular network, with node colours indicating community affiliation. (b) Laplacian spectrum of the network shown in panel (a), with graph frequencies ordered by eigenvalue. (c) First non-zero Laplacian eigenvector of the same network, representing a low-frequency mode associated with large- scale community structure. (d) Highest-frequency Laplacian eigenvector of the network, representing fine-scale variation across the graph. Together, panels (b)–(d) illustrate how the modular structure shown in panel (a) is encoded in the graph-spectral representation used throughout this work.
Fig. 3 Transfer matrix construction schematic display steps described in Section 2.3

Fig. 4 Emergence of graph-spectral cascade dynamics. (a) Temporal evolution of the modal energy Em(t), showing persistent low-frequency organisation together with intermittent redistribution across higher graph-spectral modes. Cross-sections of the transfer matrix Tm→k(t) are shown (b) outside a cascade episode and (c) during an active cascade event. Panel (d) shows the corresponding spectral flux Π(t, K0). Red vertical lines in panels (a) and (d) indicate a representative cascade episode.

Fig. 5 Comparison of synchronisation and transfer observables for a representative network realisa- tion. The figure consists of three time-dependent panels: (a) mean spectral flux Π(t) averaged over the spectral cutoff parameter K0, (b) interaction ratio Q(t), and (c) synchronisation order parameter R(t). The figure illustrates the relationship between graph-spectral transfer dynamics and global syn- chronisation. While the synchronisation order parameter remains comparatively smooth, the transfer observables exhibit pronounced fluctuations, intermittent bursts, and rapid reorganisations.
